prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of the optical lattice clock, based on magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms, which brought optical frequency standards to fractional uncertainties near 1e-18

statement.case_for: I have changed my preferred configuration from B052 to B053. The round-1 exchange did not weaken my view that aberration-corrected electron microscopy is a mature and genuinely important invention, but it showed me two things I cannot argue away. First, no other member ranks B052 first, and the objections from Danielsson, Eriksson, Johansson, Mehlig and Pearce converge on a physics-versus-method question and on the missing STEM-corrector strand (Krivanek, Dellby, Zach), which the three-name limit cannot repair. Second, I disclosed a field and user connection to B052, and the chair has noted it; placing my first preference on a candidate from my own instrument community is exactly where my judgement should count least. On the scientific merits, B053 is the candidate on which the committee's evidence is most complete. The idea is a single identifiable step: Katori's proposal of trapping neutral atoms in an optical lattice at the magic wavelength, which cancels the light shift of the clock transition while many atoms are interrogated together. The decisive demonstration is Ye's work taking such clocks to systematic uncertainties near 1e-18, about two orders of magnitude beyond the caesium standard. Independent laboratories now agree with one another at that level, so the result is reproduced and stable rather than provisional. It also reaches physics beyond metrology, through millimetre-scale gravitational redshift, bounds on drifting constants and sensitivity to certain dark-sector couplings, which speaks to the 'discovery or invention' criterion as I understand it from my own account of the statutes (as reported by Tohoku University, not an official transcript). The credited pair maps cleanly onto the achievement and all eight opening proposals gave the same two names. On the chair's first question, I believe a citation can state what is new without overreaching: lattice trapping of many neutral atoms at the magic wavelength and the resulting accuracy, not the frequency comb and not ion clocks.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection remains the one Kroll, Lindroth, Johansson and Pearce all state candidly: the lattice clock stands on the 2005 frequency-comb prize and sits beside the 2012 prize on controlled single ions, and a sceptic can call it a metrology refinement rather than a new window on nature. I judge the overlap separable but not trivial, and I accept that Mehlig and Eriksson weigh it more heavily. The two-name credit also leaves out other clock groups (Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley), and the citation must be worded so that it does not read as a priority verdict over them. Finally, the main payoff, a redefined second and decisive tests of constants, is still prospective, as Eriksson points out; Johansson is right that the case should not rest on redefinition, and I do not rest it there. Against these costs, the alternatives each carry a heavier one: unresolved allocation (B046, B009), the 2016 overlap and the Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang omission (B013), immaturity and the absent Yuan Cao (B033), the 2025 prize (B001), and my own conflict plus the STEM-corrector gap (B052).

responses.point: Kroll places B053 first on the grounds that Katori's magic-wavelength proposal and Ye's 1e-18 accuracy are cleanly separable from the frequency-comb and ion-clock prizes, with strong independent confirmation, while admitting that a lattice-clock prize could be read as metrology rather than discovery.
responses.response: In round 1 I placed B053 only third and called it my first alternative; having read Kroll's argument and the chair's summary, I now agree with him on ordering and move it to first. His point that clocks at JILA, RIKEN and Tokyo, NIST, PTB and SYRTE agree at the 1e-18 level is what persuades me on maturity, because it separates this from candidates whose central interpretive question is still open. I would ask only that the citation name the lattice scheme explicitly, so that neither the Hall and Hansch prize nor the Wineland prize can be said to be repeated. I take his discount of his own enthusiasm for precision measurement as a fair caution that applies to me as well, since I am no atomic physicist and I am relying on the accounts of those who are.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers B013 for Kane, Mele and Molenkamp as a durable organising principle not recognised in 2016, and considers the overlap of B053 with earlier clock and comb prizes closer than the 2016 overlap with B013.
responses.response: I take the conceptual weight of B013 seriously and it remains my first alternative. But the credit problem does not go away: Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang's HgTe proposal is what made the Molenkamp experiment possible, Hasan's three-dimensional work is outside the trio, and the Mele versus Molenkamp versus Hasan choice is, in my reading, a real choice rather than a drafting detail. Add the 2016 prize on topological phases, which several of us count as a cost, and I do not see a citation that is both complete and defensible in three names. On his overlap point I disagree that the lattice clock is closer to earlier work: the frequency comb is an enabling tool and the 2012 prize concerns single ions, whereas many-atom magic-wavelength trapping is a distinct physical scheme. If he can offer a draft B013 citation that handles both objections, I will reconsider the order between B013 and B053.

responses.point: Danielsson prefers the experimental Higgs discovery B046 and says he would not resist B053 if the allocation among Gianotti, Jenni, Virdee and Della Negra cannot be made defensible; about B052 he says he would want the committee clear that it judges a tool and not a finding about nature.
responses.response: His reading of B052 is fair and I no longer contest it as a ground for leading with that candidate; I now move it to second alternative. On B046 my view from round 1 stands: the science is overwhelming and I agree with him that the 2013 prize left the experimental discovery unrecognised, but choosing three of four names for a result of two collaborations of thousands is the kind of arbitrariness a citation cannot cure, and he concedes that Della Negra is as defensible as Virdee. I would only consider B046 as the preferred prize if a colleague proposes a rule for the three names that survives scrutiny and which does not simply reward the senior roles at announcement. As he says he would accept B053 on that failure, I suggest we treat the allocation question as the decision point and not reopen the scientific merit.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B033 for MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero and Bistritzer as the cleanest theory-to-experiment arc in his field, while acknowledging the unsettled pairing mechanism, device variability and the absence of Yuan Cao, and says B053 is safer on maturity.
responses.response: The prediction-then-observation arc of B033 is compelling and I concede that eight years of independent replication of the band-flattening picture is more than I had weighed. But the chair's question to him is the crux, and his own reply already answers it: the pairing mechanism is open, device-to-device variability is real, and the experimental credit rests on a group leader while the first author of the decisive experiments cannot be named under a three-person cap. A prize in this field is likely to be better placed once the superconducting mechanism and the credit allocation have settled. I note that he does not treat a B053 prize as a scandal, and that is the place where I think we can agree. On his remark that the main payoff of the clock is still prospective, I accept the point, and it is why I would word the citation around the demonstrated 1e-18 uncertainty, not the redefinition.

responses.point: Johansson now leads with B053, keeps B001 as an alternative because circuit QED is his own field and he cannot be a neutral judge, and grounds the clock case in tests of fundamental physics (redshift, varying constants) rather than redefinition of the second.
responses.response: I agree with his framing of the citation and would adopt it: the value of the clock to physics is that it tests physical law with uncertainties below 1e-18, which also answers the fair criticism that this is only metrology. His disclosure of a conflict on B001 is correct and I think the committee should treat my disclosure on B052 the same way, which is simple now that neither of us has made the conflicted candidate our first choice. I would remain cautious on B001 as a prize this year, for the reason he himself states: the missing Girvin and Devoret credit makes a three-name configuration contestable, and a second superconducting-circuit prize so soon after 2025 is a cost that I do not think the field's distinctness fully removes.

responses.point: Pearce, as chair, moved B053 to first but keeps B009 (IceCube) as his first alternative, arguing that a clock prize recognises no new window on nature and that discovery in the strict sense might outweigh invention.
responses.response: I understand his argument and it is the most serious philosophical challenge to B053 in the discussion. My difficulty with B009 is the one he names himself: the weight allocation among Halzen, Karle and Spiering, with AMANDA and Baikal outside the credited names, and several members, including Danielsson, Kroll and Mehlig, regard the source identification as still early. The statutes say discovery or invention, not discovery over invention, and a measurement technique that has opened a regime of accuracy where gravitational redshift is resolved over millimetres is closer to a new window on nature than the word metrology suggests. I accept that this is a judgement rather than a proof, and if the committee wishes to put discovery strictly first, I would want to see a three-name IceCube configuration first.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept a lattice-clock prize as a discovery or invention of the same standing as the 2005 and 2012 prizes it builds on, which depends on a citation that states the lattice scheme precisely.

How the relative weight of Katori's proposal and Ye's accuracy and many-body work should be expressed, and whether the exclusion of other clock groups (Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley) will be seen as fair.

Whether my move away from B052 is a response to the committee evidence and not to the disclosed conflict alone; I believe it is the former, since the STEM-corrector gap and the physics-versus-method question are independent of my field.
Whether B013 could overtake B053 if a citation resolves the Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang omission and the 2016 overlap, which I cannot judge from the present text.
statement.conflict_note: I am an experimental electron microscopist whose group uses aberration-corrected and in situ transmission electron microscopy, so I disclosed a field and user connection to B052, with no documented personal or institutional tie to Rose, Haider or Urban. B052 is no longer my preferred configuration and is now only my second alternative, and I would abstain from or discount my own views on B052 if the committee considers it further. I have no known tie to Katori, Ye or the lattice-clock groups, to Kane, Mele or Molenkamp, or to any other credited person, beyond ordinary field acquaintance. My Chalmers affiliation overlaps with Goran Johansson, who has disclosed his own conflict on B001, a candidate that neither of us now prefers.
